title: Book 24 — The ghosts of the suitors in Hades—Odysseus and his men go to the house of Laertes—the people of Ithaca come out to attack Odysseus, but Athena concludes a peace
paragraphs: Then Hermes of Cyllene summoned the ghosts of the suitors, holding in his hand the beautiful golden wand with which he seals men’s eyes in sleep or wakes them just as he pleases. With this he roused the ghosts and led them, while they followed him, whining and gibbering. As bats fly squealing in the hollow of some great cave when one has fallen from the cluster where they hang, so the ghosts whined and squealed as Hermes the healer of sorrow led them down into the dark abode of death. When they had passed the waters of Oceanus and the rock Leucas, they came to the gates of the sun and the land of dreams. At that they reached the meadow of asphodel where the souls and shadows of those who can labor no more dwell.
Here they found the ghost of Achilles, son of Peleus, along with those of Patroclus, Antilochus, and Ajax, who was the finest and handsomest man of all the Danaans after Peleus’s son himself.

They gathered around the ghost of Peleus’s son, and the ghost of Agamemnon joined them, grieving bitterly. Around him were also gathered the ghosts of those who had died with him in Aegisthus’s house, and Achilles’s ghost spoke first.

“Son of Atreus,” he said, “we used to say that Zeus loved you more than any other hero from beginning to end, since you commanded many brave men when we all fought together before Troy. Yet death’s hand, which no mortal can escape, struck you down far too early. It would have been better for you to have fallen at Troy at the height of your glory, for the Achaeans would have built a mound over your ashes, and your son would have inherited your good name. Instead, you were fated to meet a most wretched end.”

“Fortunate son of Peleus,” replied Agamemnon’s ghost, “for dying at Troy far from Argos, while the bravest of the Trojans and the Achaeans fell around you fighting for your body. There you lay in the swirling clouds of dust, mighty in your might, no longer troubled about your prowess in battle. We fought the entire day, and would never have stopped if Zeus had not sent a storm to halt us. Then, when we had carried you from the battle to the ships, we laid you on your bed and cleansed your fair skin with warm water and oils. The Danaans tore their hair and wept bitterly around you. Your mother, when she heard, came with her immortal nymphs from out of the sea, and the sound of great wailing went out over the waters so that the Achaeans trembled with fear. They would have fled in panic to their ships if wise old Nestor, whose counsel was always truest, had not stopped them, saying, ‘Hold fast, Argives, do not flee, sons of the Achaeans. This is his mother coming from the sea with her immortal nymphs to look upon her son’s body.’

“So he spoke, and the Achaeans feared no more. The daughters of the old man of the sea stood around you weeping bitterly and clothed you in immortal robes. The nine Muses also came and raised their sweet voices in lament, calling and answering one another. There was not an Argive who did not weep at the dirge they chanted. For seventeen days and nights we mourned you, mortals and immortals alike, but on the eighteenth day we gave you to the flames, and we sacrificed many a fat sheep and many an ox around you. You were burned in the robes of the gods, with rich resins and honey, while heroes on foot and horseback clashed their armor around the pyre as you burned, with the tramp of a great multitude. But when the flames of heaven had done their work, we gathered your white bones at daybreak and placed them in oils and pure wine. Your mother brought us a golden urn to hold them—a gift from Dionysus and the work of Hephaestus himself. In this we mingled your bleached bones with those of Patroclus, who had gone before you, and separately we enclosed those of Antilochus, who had been closer to you than any other of your comrades now that Patroclus was no more.

“Over these bones the host of the Argives built a noble tomb on a headland jutting out over the open Hellespont, so it could be seen from far out at sea by those now living and by those yet to be born. Your mother begged prizes from the gods and offered them to be competed for by the noblest of the Achaeans. You must have attended the funerals of many a hero, when young men gird themselves and make ready to compete for prizes at the death of some great chief, but you never saw such prizes as silver-footed Thetis offered in your honor, for the gods loved you well. Thus even in death your fame, Achilles, has not been lost, and your name lives forever among all mankind. But as for me, what comfort did I have when my days of fighting were done? For Zeus willed my destruction on my return, at the hands of Aegisthus and my wicked wife.”

So they talked, and presently Hermes came up to them with the ghosts of the suitors who had been killed by Odysseus. The ghosts of Agamemnon and Achilles were astonished to see them and went up to them at once. Agamemnon’s ghost recognized Amphimedon, son of Melaneus, who had lived in Ithaca and been his host, so he began to speak to him.

“Amphimedon,” he said, “what has happened to all you fine young men—all of an age too—that brings you down here under the ground? One could pick no finer group of men from any city. Did Poseidon raise his winds and waves against you when you were at sea, or did your enemies make an end of you on the mainland when you were cattle-lifting or sheep-stealing, or fighting to defend their wives and city? Answer my question, for I have been your guest. Do you not remember how I came to your house with Menelaus to persuade Odysseus to join us with his ships against Troy? It was a whole month before we could resume our voyage, for we had hard work persuading Odysseus to come with us.”

And Amphimedon’s ghost answered, “Agamemnon, son of Atreus, king of men, I remember everything you have said, and I will tell you fully and accurately how our end came about. Odysseus had been gone a long time, and we were courting his wife, who would neither refuse outright to marry nor yet bring the matter to an end, for she meant to bring about our destruction. This, then, was the trick she played us. She set up a great embroidery frame in her room and began working on an enormous piece of fine needlework. ‘Sweethearts,’ she said, ‘Odysseus is indeed dead, but do not press me to marry again just yet—wait, for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded—until I have finished a pall for the hero Laertes, ready for the time when death takes him. He is very rich, and the women of the place will talk if he is laid out without a pall.’ This is what she said, and we agreed. Then we could see her working on her great web all day long, but at night she would unpick the stitches again by torchlight. She fooled us this way for three years without our discovering it, but as time passed and she was in her fourth year, as the moons waned and many days went by, one of her maids who knew what she was doing told us, and we caught her in the act of undoing her work, so she had to finish it whether she wanted to or not. And when she showed us the robe she had made, after it had been washed, its splendor was like that of the sun or moon.

“Then some malicious god brought Odysseus to the upland farm where his swineherd lives. His son also came there, returning from a voyage to Pylos, and the two came to town after they had hatched their plot for our destruction. Telemachus came first, and then after him, accompanied by the swineherd, came Odysseus, dressed in rags and leaning on a staff like some miserable old beggar. He came so unexpectedly that none of us recognized him, not even the older ones among us, and we reviled him and threw things at him. He endured both being struck and insulted without a word, though he was in his own house. But when the will of aegis-bearing Zeus inspired him, he and Telemachus took the weapons and hid them in an inner room, bolting the doors behind them. Then he cunningly had his wife offer his bow and a quantity of iron to be competed for by us ill-fated suitors, and this was the beginning of our end, for not one of us could string the bow—we couldn’t even come close. When it was about to reach Odysseus’s hands, we all shouted that it should not be given to him, no matter what he said, but Telemachus insisted on his having it. When he got it in his hands he strung it easily and sent his arrow through the iron. Then he stood on the floor of the gallery and poured his arrows on the ground, glaring fiercely around him. First he killed Antinous, and then, aiming straight ahead, he let fly his deadly arrows and the suitors fell thick on one another. It was plain that some one of the gods was helping them, for they fell upon us with might and main throughout the gallery, and there was a hideous sound of groaning as our brains were being battered in, and the ground seethed with our blood. This, Agamemnon, is how we came by our end, and our bodies are still lying uncared for in Odysseus’s house, for our friends at home do not yet know what has happened, so they cannot lay us out and wash the black blood from our wounds, mourning over us according to the rites due to the dead.”

“Fortunate Odysseus, son of Laertes,” replied Agamemnon’s ghost, “you are indeed blessed in the possession of a wife endowed with such rare excellence of understanding, and so faithful to her wedded husband as Penelope, daughter of Icarius. The fame, therefore, of her virtue shall never die, and the immortals shall compose a song that shall be welcome to all mankind in honor of the constancy of Penelope. How far otherwise was the wickedness of the daughter of Tyndareus, who killed her lawful husband. Her song shall be hateful among men, for she has brought disgrace on all womankind, even on the good ones.”

So they talked in the house of Hades deep within the bowels of the earth. Meanwhile Odysseus and the others left the town and soon reached the fair, well-tilled farm of Laertes, which he had reclaimed with endless labor. Here was his house, with a lean-to running all around it, where the slaves who worked for him slept and sat and ate, while inside the house there was an old Sicel woman who looked after him on this country farm. When Odysseus arrived, he said to his son and the other two:
“Go to the house and kill the best pig you can find for dinner. Meanwhile I want to see whether my father will know me, or fail to recognize me after so long an absence.”

He then took off his armor and gave it to Eumaeus and Philoetius, who went straight on to the house, while he turned off into the vineyard to test his father. As he went down into the great orchard, he did not see Dolius, nor any of his sons nor the other bondservants, for they were all gathering thorns to make a fence for the vineyard at the place where the old man had told them. So he found his father alone, hoeing a vine. He wore a dirty old shirt, patched and very shabby. His legs were bound round with thongs of oxhide to save him from the brambles, and he also wore sleeves of leather. He had a goatskin cap on his head and looked very sorrowful. When Odysseus saw him so worn, so old and full of sorrow, he stood still under a tall pear tree and began to weep. He doubted whether to embrace him, kiss him, and tell him all about his having come home, or whether he should first question him and see what he would say. In the end he thought it best to be crafty with him, so with this in mind he went up to his father, who was bending down and digging around a plant.

“I see, sir,” said Odysseus, “that you are an excellent gardener—what pains you take with it, to be sure. There is not a single plant, not a fig tree, vine, olive, pear, nor flower bed, but bears the trace of your attention. I trust, however, that you will not be offended if I say that you take better care of your garden than of yourself. You are old, unkempt, and very poorly dressed. It cannot be because you are idle that your master takes such poor care of you. Indeed, your face and figure have nothing of the slave about them, and proclaim you of noble birth. I should have said that you were one of those who should wash well, eat well, and sleep comfortably at night, as old men have a right to do. But tell me truly, whose bondservant are you, and in whose garden are you working? Tell me also about another matter. Is this place that I have come to really Ithaca? I met a man just now who said so, but he was a dull fellow, and had not the patience to hear my story out when I was asking him about an old friend of mine, whether he was still living, or was already dead and in the house of Hades. Believe me when I tell you that this man came to my house once when I was in my own country, and no stranger ever came to me whom I liked better. He said that his family came from Ithaca and that his father was Laertes, son of Arceisius. I received him hospitably, welcoming him to all the abundance of my house, and when he went away I gave him all customary gifts. I gave him seven talents of fine gold, and a cup of solid silver with flowers engraved on it. I gave him twelve light cloaks, and as many pieces of tapestry. I also gave him twelve cloaks of single fold, twelve rugs, twelve fair mantles, and an equal number of shirts. To all this I added four good-looking women skilled in all useful arts, and I let him take his choice.”

His father shed tears and answered, “Sir, you have indeed come to the country that you have named, but it has fallen into the hands of wicked people. All this wealth of gifts has been given for nothing. If you could have found your friend here alive in Ithaca, he would have entertained you hospitably and would have repaid your gifts amply when you left him—as would have been only right considering what you had already given him. But tell me truly, how many years is it since you entertained this guest—my unhappy son, if ever there was one? Alas! He has perished far from his own country. The fish of the sea have eaten him, or he has fallen prey to the birds and wild beasts of some land. We who were his parents, his mother and I his father, could not throw our arms about him and wrap him in his shroud, nor could his excellent and richly dowered wife Penelope mourn her husband as was proper at his deathbed, and close his eyes according to the rites due to the dead. But now, tell me truly, for I want to know: Who are you and where do you come from? Tell me of your city and parents. Where is the ship lying that has brought you and your men to Ithaca? Or were you a passenger on someone else’s ship, and those who brought you here have gone on their way and left you?”

“I will tell you everything,” answered Odysseus, “quite truthfully. I come from Alybas, where I have a fine house. I am the son of King Apheidas, who is the son of Polypemon. My own name is Eperitus. Heaven drove me off my course as I was leaving Sicania, and I have been carried here against my will. As for my ship, it is lying over yonder, off the open country outside the town, and this is the fifth year since Odysseus left my country. Poor fellow, yet the omens were good for him when he left me. The birds all flew on our right hands, and both he and I rejoiced to see them as we parted, for we had every hope that we should have another friendly meeting and exchange gifts.”

A dark cloud of sorrow fell upon Laertes as he listened. He filled both hands with dust from the ground and poured it over his gray head, groaning heavily as he did so. Odysseus’s heart was touched, and his nostrils quivered as he looked upon his father. Then he sprang toward him, threw his arms around him and kissed him, saying, “I am he, father, the one you are asking about—I have returned after being away for twenty years. But stop your sighing and weeping—we have no time to lose, for I should tell you that I have been killing the suitors in my house, to punish them for their insolence and crimes.”
“If you really are my son Odysseus,” replied Laertes, “and have come back again, you must give me such manifest proof of your identity as will convince me.”

“First look at this scar,” answered Odysseus, “which I got from a boar’s tusk when I was hunting on Mount Parnassus. You and my mother had sent me to Autolycus, my mother’s father, to receive the gifts he had promised to give me when he was here. Furthermore, I will point out to you the trees in the vineyard which you gave me, and I asked you about them all as I followed you around the garden. We went over them all, and you told me their names and what they all were. You gave me thirteen pear trees, ten apple trees, and forty fig trees. You also said you would give me fifty rows of vines, with corn planted between each row, and they yield grapes of every kind when the heat of heaven lies heavy upon them.”

Laertes’s strength failed him when he heard the convincing proofs his son had given him. He threw his arms around him, and Odysseus had to support him, or he would have gone off into a swoon. But as soon as he came to, and was beginning to recover his senses, he said, “O father Zeus, then you gods are still on Olympus after all, if the suitors have really been punished for their insolence and folly. Nevertheless, I am much afraid that I shall have all the townspeople of Ithaca up here directly, and they will be sending messengers everywhere throughout the cities of the Cephallenians.”

Odysseus answered, “Take heart and do not trouble yourself about that, but let us go into the house near your garden. I have already told Telemachus, Philoetius, and Eumaeus to go there and get dinner ready as soon as possible.”

So the two made their way toward the house, talking together. When they got there they found Telemachus with the stockman and the swineherd cutting up meat and mixing wine with water. Then the old Sicel woman took Laertes inside and washed him and anointed him with oil. She put a good cloak on him, and Athena came up to him and gave him a more imposing presence, making him taller and stouter than before. When he came back his son was surprised to see him looking so like an immortal, and said to him, “My dear father, some one of the gods has been making you much taller and better-looking.”

Laertes answered, “If only, by Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo, I were the man I was when I ruled among the Cephallenians, and took Nericum, that strong fortress on the foreland. If I were still the man I was then, and had been in our house yesterday with my armor on, I should have been able to stand by you and help you against the suitors. I should have killed a great many of them, and you would have rejoiced to see it.”

So they talked, but the others, when they had finished their work and the feast was ready, stopped working, and each took his proper place on the benches and seats. Then they began eating. By and by old Dolius and his sons left their work and came up, for their mother, the Sicel woman who looked after Laertes now that he was growing old, had gone to fetch them. When they saw Odysseus and were certain it was he, they stood there lost in astonishment. But Odysseus scolded them good-naturedly and said, “Sit down to your dinner, old man, and never mind about your surprise. We have been wanting to begin for some time and have been waiting for you.”

Then Dolius stretched out both his hands and went up to Odysseus. “Sir,” he said, seizing his master’s hand and kissing it at the wrist, “we have long been wishing you home: and now heaven has restored you to us after we had given up hoping. Welcome, then, and may the gods prosper you. But tell me, does Penelope already know of your return, or shall we send someone to tell her?”

“Old man,” answered Odysseus, “she knows already, so you need not trouble about that.” At this he took his seat, and Dolius’s sons gathered around Odysseus to give him greeting and embrace him one after the other. Then they took their seats in due order near Dolius their father.

While they were thus busy getting their dinner ready, Rumor went around the town and spread news of the terrible fate that had befallen the suitors. As soon, therefore, as the people heard of it, they gathered from every quarter, groaning and wailing before Odysseus’s house. They took the dead away, each man burying his own, and put the bodies of those who came from elsewhere on board the fishing vessels, for the fishermen to take each of them to his own place. They then met angrily in the assembly place, and when they were gathered together Eupeithes rose to speak. He was overwhelmed with grief for the death of his son Antinous, who had been the first man killed by Odysseus, so he said, weeping bitterly, “My friends, this man has done the Achaeans great wrong. He took many of our best men away with him in his fleet, and he has lost both ships and men. Now, moreover, on his return he has been killing all the foremost men among the Cephallenians. Let us be up and doing before he can get away to Pylos or to Elis, where the Epeans rule, or we shall be ashamed of ourselves forever. It will be an everlasting disgrace to us if we do not avenge the murder of our sons and brothers. For my own part I would have no more pleasure in life, but would rather die at once. Let us be up, then, and after them, before they can cross over to the mainland.”

He wept as he spoke, and everyone pitied him. But Medon and the bard Phemius had now awakened, and came to them from Odysseus’s house. Everyone was astonished at seeing them, but they stood in the middle of the assembly, and Medon said, “Hear me, men of Ithaca. Odysseus did not do these things against the will of heaven. I myself saw an immortal god take the form of Mentor and stand beside him. This god appeared, now in front of him encouraging him, and now going furiously about the court and attacking the suitors, at which they fell thick on one another.”

At this pale fear laid hold of them, and old Halitherses, son of Mastor, rose to speak, for he was the only man among them who knew both past and future. So he spoke to them plainly and in all honesty, and said:

“Men of Ithaca, it is all your own fault that things have turned out as they have. You would not listen to me, nor yet to Mentor, when we told you to check the folly of your sons, who were doing much wrong in the wantonness of their hearts—wasting the wealth and dishonoring the wife of a chief who they thought would not return. Now, however, let it be as I say, and do as I tell you. Do not go out against Odysseus, or you may find that you have been bringing evil down upon your own heads.”

This was what he said, and more than half raised a loud shout, and at once left the assembly. But the rest stayed where they were, for the speech of Halitherses displeased them, and they sided with Eupeithes. They therefore hurried off for their weapons, and when they had armed themselves, they met together in front of the city, and Eupeithes led them on in their folly. He thought he was going to avenge the murder of his son, but in truth he was never to return, and was himself to perish in the attempt.
Then Athena said to Zeus, “Father, son of Cronus, king of kings, answer me this question—What do you propose to do? Will you set them fighting still further, or will you make peace between them?”

And Zeus answered, “My child, why should you ask me? Was it not by your own arrangement that Odysseus came home and took his revenge upon the suitors? Do whatever you like, but I will tell you what I think will be the most reasonable arrangement. Now that Odysseus is revenged, let them swear to a solemn covenant, by which he shall continue to rule, while we cause the others to forgive and forget the massacre of their sons and brothers. Let them then all become friends as before, and let peace and plenty reign.”
This was what Athena was already eager to bring about, so she darted down from the highest peaks of Olympus.

Now when Laertes and the others had finished dinner, Odysseus began by saying, “Some of you go out and see if they are not getting close up to us.” So one of Dolius’s sons went as he was told. Standing on the threshold he could see them all quite near, and said to Odysseus, “Here they are, let us put on our armor at once.”

They armed themselves as fast as they could—that is to say Odysseus, his three men, and the six sons of Dolius. Laertes also and Dolius did the same—warriors by necessity in spite of their gray hair. When they had all put on their armor, they opened the gate and marched out, Odysseus leading the way.

Then Zeus’s daughter Athena came up to them, having assumed the form and voice of Mentor. Odysseus was glad when he saw her, and said to his son Telemachus, “Telemachus, now that you are about to fight in an engagement that will show every man’s mettle, be sure not to disgrace your ancestors, who were eminent for their strength and courage the world over.”
“You say truly, my dear father,” answered Telemachus, “and you shall see, if you will, that I am in no mind to disgrace your family.”
Laertes was delighted when he heard this. “Good heavens,” he exclaimed, “what a day I am enjoying! I do indeed rejoice at it. My son and grandson are competing with each other in courage.”
At this Athena came close up to him and said, “Son of Arceisius—best friend I have in the world—pray to the blue-eyed maiden Athena, and to Zeus her father, then poise your spear and hurl it.”

As she spoke she filled him with fresh vigor, and when he had prayed to her he poised his spear and hurled it. He struck Eupeithes’s helmet, and the spear went right through it, for the helmet did not stop it, and his armor rang rattling around him as he fell heavily to the ground. Meanwhile Odysseus and his son fell upon the front line of the foe and struck them down with their swords and spears. Indeed, they would have killed every one of them, and prevented them from ever getting home again, but Athena raised her voice aloud, and made everyone pause. “Men of Ithaca,” she cried, “cease this dreadful war, and settle the matter at once without further bloodshed.”

At this pale fear seized everyone. They were so frightened that their weapons dropped from their hands and fell upon the ground at the sound of the goddess’s voice, and they fled back to the city for their lives. But Odysseus gave a great cry, and gathering himself together, swooped down like a soaring eagle. Then the son of Cronus sent a thunderbolt of fire that fell just in front of Athena, so she said to Odysseus, “Odysseus, noble son of Laertes, stop this warlike strife, or Zeus will be angry with you.”
So spoke Athena, and Odysseus obeyed her gladly. Then Athena assumed the form and voice of Mentor, and presently made a covenant of peace between the two contending parties.
